name: Piscataway
confidence_why: Piscataway survives only in Andrew White's seventeenth-century catechism, and Mackie (2006), the sole description, says the acute and grave marks "could indicate word stress" (wúnnay with initial stress) but also sit on apparently monosyllabic words and leaves the prosody "a subject for further study", so no stress placement or type can be stated.

new_statements.quote: The diacritics in the text are acute, grave, circumflex, umlaut, hook, and a dot placed below certain letters. There are also combinations of diacritics. The acute and grave diacritics could indicate word stress. (It is possible that White was familiar with the stress accent marks of Spanish.) For example, wúnnay from the Pater Noster could be a two-syllable word with stress on the first syllable. However, there are cases of words which are probably monosyllabic and would not require a stress accent, for example äPp which has both an umlaut and a grave diacritic. In these cases, it seems more likely that the diacritics indicate a quality of the vowel or consonant. Undoubtedly there is a great deal of information conveyed by this system of diacritics but it remains a subject for further study.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule can be stated. The only record of the language is a five-page 17th-century catechism by Fr. Andrew White; its acute/grave marks might be stress marks (one example would then show initial stress), but because apparently monosyllabic words also carry them the author concludes they more likely mark segment quality, and leaves the prosody undetermined. Tone/pitch accent is explicitly judged 'remote' (p. 88).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source declines to establish any stress pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Data are written prayer texts (Sign of the Cross, Pater Noster, Ave Maria, Creed, Commandments), so no citation forms or phrase-level information; the diacritics discussed are orthographic marks in a single manuscript.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the language of a single five-page Jesuit catechism (Georgetown University Library) attributed to Fr. Andrew White; identification as Piscataway/Conoy (pisc1239) rests on that attribution (Mackie 2006 abstract and §1.3). Nanticoke (nant1249) is a distinct Glottolog language and Speck 1927's 'Nanticoke and Conoy' vocabulary material is Nanticoke, not this text.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Piscataway Phonetics and Phonology', §5.3 Diacritics pp. 88-89: the acute and grave marks in Fr. Andrew White's c.1634-40 catechism 'could indicate word stress' (example wúnnay, possibly disyllable with initial stress), but since apparent monosyllables also carry them the diacritics more likely mark vowel/consonant quality; the possibility that they mark tone/pitch accent is judged 'remote'; the whole system 'remains a subject for further study'. Conclusion p. 112 repeats that 'the prosodic properties of the language' are unresolved. No stress rule is stated.
